claims.text: The primary mechanism of corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is formation of a stable, self-healing Cr2O3 passivation layer.
Chromium diffuses from the steel to its surface under oxidizing conditions.
Surface chromium oxidizes to form Cr2O3.
The Cr2O3 layer prevents corrosive species from reaching the underlying metal.
After local damage, chromium diffusion re-establishes the Cr2O3 film.
Re-establishment of the damaged film slows or prevents further corrosion.
Steels with sufficient chromium content should develop a uniform and stable Cr2O3 passive film.
Steels with sufficient chromium content should have significantly lower corrosion rates than steels with lower chromium content.
The lower corrosion rate should appear as reduced weight loss and fewer pitting sites.
Breakdown or failure of the passive film should correlate with increased corrosion.
Lower-chromium steels should have higher corrosion rates under the same exposure conditions.
Samples pretreated to remove their oxide layer should have higher corrosion rates under the same exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate within the selected temperature, chemical-exposure, and radiation-dose ranges representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
Extreme mechanical wear or temperature cycling that destroys the passive layer may allow other corrosion mechanisms to dominate.
The critical chromium concentration required for optimal passivation is not yet quantified in the hypothesis.
Possible synergistic effects of other alloying elements, including molybdenum, remain unresolved.
The combined effects of radiation and chemical attack on Cr2O3-layer stability remain unresolved.
